24 V control: read R to C at the board with everything calling; a drop from ~27 V unloaded to < 20 V loaded = overloaded transformer or a high-resistance connection in the chain. Voltage drops across individual safeties (read across each switch): 24 V across a switch = it is open; ~0 V = closed.
Infrared or touch check: warm lugs, discolored insulation, and melted terminal blocks are high-resistance connections; re-terminate and torque to spec.
Source: NEC 210.19 informational note (3 % branch, 5 % total recommended); manufacturer service manuals.

reference.topic: Electrical safety: LOTO, live-dead-live, meter categories, arc flash, capacitors, A2L
content: Lockout/tagout per NFPA 70E and OSHA 1910.147: open the disconnect, apply your lock and tag, try to start the unit, and verify zero energy. A pulled fuse block is not a lockout.

Live-dead-live: prove the meter on a known live source, test every conductor to be touched (line-to-line and line-to-ground on all legs), then re-prove the meter on the live source. A dead meter battery or a blown meter fuse reads 0 V on a live circuit.

Meter category: use CAT III (600 V) minimum for 208/240 V equipment and CAT III 1000 V / CAT IV 600 V rated meters and leads for 480/575 V distribution; fused test leads; never measure amps with the meter leads in the voltage jacks.

Arc-flash: measuring live 480/575 V in an open panel is energized work — arc-rated PPE (category per the label/incident-energy study), face shield, insulating gloves; keep the body out of the line of the panel; work de-energized whenever possible.

Capacitors: discharge every run and start capacitor through a bleed resistor (≈ 20 kΩ, 5 W) before touching terminals or removing leads; VFD DC buses need the manual's discharge time and a measured < 50 VDC before entry.

A2L refrigerants (R-32, R-454B): no ignition sources (open flame, non-rated electrical tools, sparking contactors with the panel open) when a leak is suspected or mitigation is active; ventilate; A2L-rated recovery/vacuum/leak-detection equipment; never defeat the RDS.
Rooftop hazards: fall protection near edges/hatches, wind on panels/doors, hot surfaces (discharge lines > 200 °F, motors), and condenser fans starting without warning.
Source: NFPA 70E (Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147; UL 60335-2-40 / ASHRAE 15 for A2L systems.

reference.topic: 24 V control path tracing (safety chain method)
content: Typical cooling safety chain order (verify on the unit's ladder diagram): control transformer secondary (TRAN) → control fuse/breaker (3 A) → board R terminal → thermostat/BAS call on Y → high-pressure switch (HPS) → low-pressure/loss-of-charge switch (LPS/LOC) → freeze stat → condensate overflow switch → duct smoke detector(s) → fire-alarm/shutdown relay → phase monitor contact → anti-short-cycle timer → compressor contactor coil (C/CC) and back to C (common).

Method: with the call active, put the meter's common lead on C and walk the hot lead along the chain — 24 V is present up to the open device and 0 V after it. Alternatively read ACROSS each device: ~0 V = closed, 24 V = the opener.
Boards with dedicated inputs: many modern boards wire each safety to its own input and show a code (HPS open, LPS open, freeze, condensate) — read the code first, then measure.

Momentary diagnostic jumper: a jumper across a suspected open switch, applied attended and for seconds only, confirms the opener; it is never a fix and never left in place. Never jumper rollout/limit/pressure switches on gas heat or the RDS on A2L units.

Grounded common: on many units C is chassis-grounded; a 24 V wire chafed to the cabinet blows the control fuse — a fuse that blows immediately on power = short; that blows on the call = a shorted coil/actuator in that circuit.
Source: manufacturer IOM/service manuals (ladder diagrams and legends); ACCA/NATE service fundamentals.

A ladder diagram shows power on the two vertical rails (line voltage on the upper section, 24 V on the lower section, separated by the transformer) and each load on a horizontal rung with its controls (switches, contacts, safeties) in series to its left.

Contacts are drawn in their de-energized, shelf state: a normally-open (NO) contact is open until its coil is energized; a normally-closed (NC) contact conducts until energized. Pressure/temperature switches are drawn at atmospheric/room conditions.

Designators: C/CC (compressor contactor), OFC/OFR (outdoor fan), IFC/IFR (indoor fan), TRAN (transformer), HPS/LPS (pressure switches), LS (limit), RS (rollout), FS (freeze stat), CH (crankcase heater), IGC (ignition control), DFB (defrost board), ECON (economizer), PM (phase monitor), TDR (time delay relay). Every legend is unit-specific — read the legend on the diagram.
Match the wiring diagram (physical layout, wire colors, terminal numbers) with the ladder (logic) to find where a wire physically runs.
Sequence of operation text in the IOM tells what should happen in what order; use it as the checklist while tracing.
Source: manufacturer wiring diagrams (inside the unit's control-panel door) and IOMs.

Thermostat wire colors (R red, C blue/black, Y yellow, G green, W white, O/B orange/dark blue) are conventions, not rules — a previous tech may have used any color. Verify at both ends with a meter before trusting a color.

Line voltage: black/red/blue for phases, white for neutral (120 V), green/bare for ground in North America; 480 V often uses brown/orange/yellow with gray neutral. Factory harness colors in units follow the diagram's color codes (e.g. 'BLK', 'YEL', 'VIO' abbreviations on the diagram).

Replacement components can come with different lead colors than the diagram (ECM motors, capacitors, transformers with multi-tap primaries: black common, red 240 V, orange 208 V, etc. — check the transformer label).
Faded/sun-bleached wires on rooftops (orange looks yellow, red looks pink) — use the terminal number, not the shade.
Never assume a white wire is neutral inside a unit: it is frequently a hot leg or the 24 V W heat call.
Source: manufacturer diagrams; NEC 200.6/210.5 identification requirements.

reference.topic: Megohm (insulation resistance) testing of compressors and motors
content: Test at 500 VDC (hermetic compressors and motors up to 600 V), leads removed, each terminal to a clean ground on the shell/discharge line. Take the reading after ~60 s.

Bands (general field guidance, IEEE 43 style): > 100 MΩ good; 20–100 MΩ investigate (moisture, acid, contaminated oil — check the oil/acid test, drier, moisture indicator, re-test after run time); < 20 MΩ suspect winding insulation breakdown; < 1 MΩ condemn (grounded winding; treat the system as contaminated/burnout).

Copeland AE4-1294 (Megohm Values of Copeland Compressors): ≥ 0.5 MΩ acceptable on a new, never-installed compressor; 0.5–20 MΩ on an installed compressor = contaminated system — clean up (driers, oil change) and re-test rather than condemn; < 0.5 MΩ = condemn.

Readings are affected by refrigerant dissolved in the oil (lower when cold and just after shutdown), temperature (rise as the compressor warms) and moisture. Trend readings over time rather than relying on a single number; compare all three terminals.

Never megger in a vacuum: the thin gas inside the shell ionizes and arcs to the shell, damaging the motor. Never megger with a VFD or electronic control connected — it destroys the drive's output stage. Discharge the winding after the test.
Source: Copeland/Emerson AE4-1294 R1 (Megohm Values of Copeland Compressors) and Copeland KB a_id 763/785 for the 0.5 MΩ limits; IEEE 43 general practice for the 100/20/1 MΩ field bands.

Under-load capacitance: µF = 2652 × A / V, with amps clamped on the capacitor's HERM (or FAN) lead only and volts read across that capacitor section while the motor runs. The constant 2652 comes from 1 / (2π × 60 Hz) × 10⁶.
The measurement is invalid on the compressor common lead or line lead (reads far too high) — on a dual capacitor test the HERM and FAN sections separately.
Tolerance: ±6 % of the rating printed on the can unless the can states otherwise (±5 %, ±10 %); start capacitors are −0 / +20 % of the printed minimum.
Bench test: discharge, remove leads, capacitance meter; replace on bulge, leak, or rust regardless of the reading. Voltage rating equal or higher, µF the same.
Source: capacitor manufacturer data (Genteq/Titan/AmRad), Copeland AE bulletins on PSC/CSR compressor starting components.

reference.topic: VFD measurements and first checks by fault
content: Output voltage from a PWM drive cannot be read accurately with a standard true-RMS meter — use output current (balanced within 10 % of each other, below motor FLA) or a meter with a low-pass filter / VFD mode. The keypad's output frequency and current are the reference.

Fault first checks: OC (over-current) → shorted motor/cable, mechanical binding, accel too fast, wrong motor data; OV (over-voltage) → decel too fast, regenerating load, high line; UV (under-voltage) → line sag, loose input lug, blown input fuse, weak bus caps; OH (over-temperature) → heatsink/fan clogged, high ambient, enclosure ventilation; GF (ground fault) → motor or cable insulation (megger with the drive DISCONNECTED).
Before touching: open the disconnect, wait the manual's discharge time, measure the DC bus < 50 VDC, and verify the input and the bypass contactor are dead (live-dead-live).

Motor won't ramp: check run enable/safety input, HOA in AUTO, speed reference present at the terminals (0–10 V / 4–20 mA), min/max frequency parameters, and PID setpoint/feedback (static pressure transducer) before suspecting the drive.
Source: drive manufacturer manuals (ABB ACH, Danfoss FC, Yaskawa); NFPA 70E for stored-energy verification.

Terminals: C (common), S (start), R (run). Resistances: R(S-R) = R(C-S) + R(C-R); C-R (run winding) is the lowest reading, C-S (start winding) the higher single winding, S-R the highest (the two in series). Typical values 0.5–5 Ω; use a low-ohms meter and clean pins.
Open C-S and C-R with an intact S-R = the internal line-break overload (in series with common) is open — the compressor is hot; cool 1–2 hours and re-test before condemning.
Mismatch of the sum by more than ~10 % or an unexpected order = shorted turns or mis-identified pins; verify the pin layout from the compressor label/terminal cover.
Identify unmarked pins: the pair with the highest resistance excludes common; the remaining pin is C; from C, the lower reading is R, the higher is S.
Source: Copeland/Emerson AE bulletins (single-phase compressor electrical checks); Tecumseh service handbook.
